“Italy has plenty of sun, but it still runs its evenings on expensive gas – batteries can change that.”

Italy’s reliance on sky-high gas prices could be eased by a boom in battery storage, helping lower energy bills for cash-strapped households.

Despite achieving 49 per cent of its electricity share from renewable sources last year, the country is still dependent on gas – the most expensive way to generate electricity – when demand is at its highest.

This tends to be around 8pm when people come home from work and school, which coincides with a dip in solar generation due to a lack of sunlight.

A new analysis from energy think tank Ember, in collaboration with Cleantech for Italy and Energy Square, found pairing solar and wind power with battery storage systems (BESS) is becoming central to Italy’s power system – and the country needs to act fast.

How batteries can slash Italy’s electricity prices

The study found that even under conservative estimates, renewable power stored and shifted to the evening could cost €106/MW against €210/MWh for gas power at October 2026 gas prices.

This means that battery storage could cut electricity prices by up to 49 per cent compared to producing electricity with a typical gas power plant.

“Italy has plenty of sun, but it still runs its evenings on expensive gas,” says Beatrice Petrovich, a principal energy analyst at Ember.

“Batteries change that, carrying low-cost renewable power into the hours when prices peak. Italy is already one of the most advanced EU countries for batteries connected to the power grid."

If Italy gets the rules right, accelerating on storage and renewables will mean lower power prices for consumers.”

Batteries met an average of 2.8 per cent of Italy’s peak demand in the first half of 2026, more than double the level in the first half of last year, and are already displacing soaring gas prices.

This may seem small in comparison to fossil power’s 40 per cent, but analysts say it could grow quickly as contracted projects start to come online.

This is already happening across the EU, as nations scramble to balance renewable power and reduce curtailment (when clean energy is wasted due to supply outstripping demand).

Take Bulgaria, which has grown its grid-scale battery fleet from almost nothing in 2024 to almost 3 GWh by the end of 2025 and 16 GWh by August 2026 – overtaking Italy despite having a much smaller power system.

In the first half of 2026, batteries routinely supplied over a quarter of Bulgaria’s electricity demand (28 per cent) during the 8pm evening demand peak, up from four per cent one year prior, while fossil power’s share of the evening peak fell from 35 per cent to 31 per cent.

Bulgaria experienced less extreme price spikes during the summer 2026 heatwave than neighbouring countries, with strong battery discharge being one of the main drivers.

‘Storage and new generation need to develop together’

The price of electricity remains tied to volatile fossil fuels due to what is known as the merit order principle.

This ensures that electricity prices are based on the most expensive power plant still needed to meet demand.

So, if Italy’s electricity needs cannot be covered solely by clean energy (which it can’t when there is a lack of wind and sunshine), more expensive sources like coal or gas step in.

As Michele Torsello, director of Energy Square, points out – Italy’s challenge therefore isn’t to simply install more batteries, but to build an electricity system that “makes the most” of renewable energy.

“Storage, grids and new generation need to develop together,” he adds.

“As renewables grow, the value of each investment increasingly depends on the others. Capturing these synergies is key to translating this progress into lower costs for the electricity system as a whole.”

Informația a fost confirmată și de Brave 1, un grup format din mai multe companii care dezvoltă tehnologii militare ucrainene. Serhii Beskrestnov, consilier al președintelui, a anunțat că laserul a fost utilizat pentru a proteja o infrastructură critică, iar imaginile publicate online arată o dronă care se prăbușește și explodează după interceptare.

Sistemul Blysk este “o armă cu energie dirijată”, care folosește un fascicul laser concentrat pentru a încălzi și distruge structura dronei, în loc să lanseze o rachetă interceptoare. Compania dezvoltatoare susține că laserul poate focaliza asupra unui punct al țintei și poate perfora fuselajul unei drone de tip Shahed în câteva secunde. Sistemul are o putere de aproximativ 4 kilowați și o rază de acțiune raportată de circa 800 de metri, fiind mult mai puțin puternic decât sistemul israelian Iron Beam, care are o putere de 100 de kilowați și este conceput pentru interceptarea dronelor, rachetelor și obuzelor de mortier la distanțe de până la aproximativ 10 kilometri.

Ucraina investește în dezvoltarea armelor laser, considerate o posibilă alternativă mai ieftină la rachetele antiaeriene, care sunt costisitoare și ale căror stocuri sunt limitate. Aceste sisteme pot fi reutilizate, consumând în principal energie electrică, însă eficiența lor este influențată de condițiile meteorologice, precum ceața, norii sau precipitațiile. Laserul Blysk fusese desfășurat în sistemul de apărare al Kievului de la începutul lunii noiembrie, dar nu a putut fi testat în condiții favorabile până în această săptămână, potrivit presei britanice.

Dezvoltarea tehnologiei face parte din programul ucrainean “Private Air Defense”, în cadrul căruia aproximativ 100 de companii participă la dezvoltarea unor tehnologii de apărare. Kievul încearcă să găsească soluții suplimentare pentru apărarea orașelor și infrastructurii, în condițiile în care președintele Volodimir Zelenski a avertizat în repetate rânduri asupra deficitului de interceptoare pentru rachetele balistice, inclusiv cele furnizate de sistemele Patriot.

The winter solstice falls on the shortest day and the longest night of the year, and across Europe this is marked with celebrations steeped in tradition.

Europe’s winter calendar isn’t just about chilly temperatures, cream-topped cups of hot chocolate and donning gloves. Across the continent, the festive season is also a time to observe the winter solstice.

The astronomical event marking the shortest day and longest night of the year in the Northern Hemisphere derives its name from the Latin word “sōlstitium”, which means the “sun stands still”.

While the December date it’s celebrated on varies slightly from country to country in Europe, centuries-old traditions are what’s common, including bonfires and parades to ward away the gloom and doom of the year and ushering in new beginnings and light.

From England to Latvia, the occasion continues to draw visitors. Here’s where to set off to in Europe if you have your sights on celebrating the winter solstice.

Must-visit destinations for the Winter Solstice

Stone Circle at Stonehenge, England

One of Europe’s most iconic destinations to observe the winter solstice is at Stonehenge’s Stone Circle.

The mysterious monument, which has a history spanning 4,500 years from the Neolithic and Bronze Age, may have been built especially to mark the occasion with experts noting that the stones are shaped and set up to frame the midwinter sunset at the time of winter solstice.

Archaeologists also estimate that Neolithic people may have gathered at Stonehenge during the winter solstice to have feasts and take part in celebrations.

On 22 December 2026, sunrise in Stonehenge will be at 8:09 am and entry will be free for the scores of spiritualists and tourists that will gather for the year’s shortest day.

The ‘Old Solstice’ in northern Europe and Nordic countries

Observed on 13 December in countries like Sweden, Finland, Denmark and Norway, St. Lucia’s day is a Scandinavian and Nordic tradition to usher in light during the darkest days of the year.

With roots in both Christian and older Norse folkloric tradition, the occasion honours the martyrdom of St. Lucia, whose name means “light”. The date originates from medieval Scandinavia’s winter solstice according to the Julian Calendar.

In Sweden, “Luciatåg” processions are broadcast on national television as well as held across the country’s schools, churches, town halls and celebrated in homes and offices. Observes dress in white robes and a young girl portrays the Saint, wearing a crown and holding a candle.

In Helsinki, Finland, the Lucia crowning ceremony and parade attracts around 30,000 people each year. A young girl is chosen to represent Saint Lucia and given the duty of leading parades through the city.

Meanwhile in Norway, “Lucia-dagen” is marked with the tradition of eating “lussekatt” s-shaped buns, baked with saffron. Traditionally only eaten on St. Lucia’s Day, the yellow colour was once associated with light, purity and protection from evil in medieval Europe.

Koliada in Slavic countries

In countries like Czechia and Poland, you may catch parades of people dressed as goats, bulls and even evil spirits as part of Koliada, or Koleda as it’s otherwise known, celebrations.

Also having roots as a pre-Christian festival to mark the winter solstice, in ancient times, a procession of young people, called “the koledari” in Czechia, dressed in costumes that were thought to ward off demons.

They would also sing carols for each house they passed by to cleanse it, and, in turn, homeowners would give them sweets and money.

**Newgrange, Ireland **

This mysterious kidney-shaped mount in County Meath, Ireland, is thought to have once served as a religious and ceremonial hub among Neolithic people and took 300 people to build over 20 years.

One of the oldest astronomically-oriented structures in the world, a beam of light spears into the roof-box and reaches up to 19 metres along the passage and illuminates the chamber during the mornings of the winter solstice. This happens from 19-23 December each year and lasts for 17 minutes.

The ancient ceremony has a limited capacity, with a controlled lottery selecting fewer than 40 people who can come accompanied by a guest to witness the solar phenomenon.

**Yule Logs, Latvia **

Across Latvia, it’s tradition to don a mask and drag a yule log around one’s home or neighbourhood before burning it in a communal fire to mark the solstice on 21 December.

This is thought to represent shedding the hardship, adversities and misfortunes of the soon-to-be previous year and chase away evil spirits.

In the country’s capital, Rīga, at the Town Hall in the old town, this tradition unfolds with singing, dancing and traditional Latvian games as the symbolic log is rolled through several streets before being burned in a large bonfire.

Yuri Grekhov, 64, who oversaw procurement of aircraft, missiles and air defence systems and has been under EU sanctions since 2022, is a serving officer, unlike most of the more than a dozen senior defence figures detained since Andrei Belousov replaced Sergei Shoigu as defence minister in 2024.

Russia has arrested Aerospace Forces (VKS) Deputy Commander in Chief Yuri Grekhov on charges of accepting a particularly large bribe, the latest in a series of corruption cases against senior military figures since the country changed its defence minister in 2024.

Grekhov, 64, oversaw procurement of aircraft, munitions, missiles and air defence systems. The charge carries a prison sentence of up to 15 years under Russian law.

Grekhov has been on the EU sanctions list since 2022, when Brussels deemed him responsible for Russian strikes on military and civilian sites after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

A career military officer since 1979, Grekhov became deputy commander in chief under Alexander Chaiko in 2021, after commanding the air and missile defence forces from 2018 to 2021.

Unlike most of the other officials detained in recent cases, Grekhov is a serving officer, making him one of the most senior figures to come under investigation while still in post.

The VKS controls Russia's military aviation, space operations and strategic missile defence, and has played a central role in strikes on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure throughout the war.

String of arrests since Shoigu's removal

At least a dozen senior ministry employees and generals have been detained or become criminal suspects since Andrei Belousov replaced the dismissed Sergei Shoigu as defence minister in 2024.

Belousov, an economist with no military background, was appointed with an explicit mandate to impose financial discipline on the defence ministry in what Moscow said was part of a crackdown on corruption within military ranks.

The most prominent case was the arrest of former Deputy Defence Minister Timur Ivanov in April 2024.

A close associate of Shoigu for more than a decade, Ivanov was convicted of taking a particularly large bribe in Defence Ministry contracting work, embezzlement and money laundering. He was sentenced to 13 years in a penal colony and fined 100 million roubles (€1 million).

Former first deputy defence minister Ruslan Tsalikov was detained in March 2026 on charges of creating a criminal organisation, embezzlement and laundering budget funds. In November he received 10 years in a high-security penal colony and a fine of 500 million roubles (€5 million).

Others detained for bribery and embezzlement include former Deputy Chief of the General Staff Vadim Shamarin, sentenced to seven years, former head of the Defence Ministry's Main Personnel Directorate Yuri Kuznetsov, sentenced to 12 years, and former Deputy Defence Ministers Dmitry Bulgakov and Pavel Popov.

Several Western governments have assessed that the prosecutions also serve to selectively remove officials who have fallen out of favour with the Kremlin.

The pattern of cases allows Moscow to present itself as enforcing accountability while using criminal charges as a tool of internal political control.

Unemployment among 15- to 24-year-olds in the EU is three times the rate among people aged 25 to 74. Where in Europe is youth unemployment highest, and what helps explain the gap between the two age groups?

In Bosnia and Herzegovina, nearly one in three economically active 15- to 24-year-olds were unemployed in the second quarter of 2026. That was the highest rate among the countries analysed. In Malta, which had the lowest rate, the figure was about one in 15. Across the EU, it was about one in six.

If we compare the two age groups, the EU youth unemployment rate was 15.6% in the same period, three times the rate for 25- to 74-year-olds (5.2%), according to Eurostat.

The rate covers only people in the labour force, meaning those who are working or actively looking for work.

That gap varies widely across Europe. In Poland, for example, youth unemployment was below the EU rate, yet it was more than four times the rate among 25- to 74-year-olds. Where is the gap widest, and what helps explain it?

Youth unemployment is highest in the Balkans

Among the 35 European countries in the data, youth unemployment is highest in Bosnia and Herzegovina at 32.2%. Romania (30.7%) and North Macedonia (29%) follow.

Countries where at least one in five young people in the labour force cannot find a job include Sweden (24.9%), Serbia (24.2%), Spain (23.9%), Finland (23.2%), Estonia (22.8%), France (21.6%) and Croatia (20%).

In these countries, many young people struggle to find a first job and gain the work experience that employers ask for.

Youth unemployment is lowest in Malta and Germany

Malta (6.8%) and Germany (7.3%) have the lowest rates. The Netherlands (8.6%), Switzerland (9.2%) and Austria (9.7%) are also below 10%.

Youth unemployment also varies widely among the EU's four largest economies. While the rate is 7.3% in Germany, it is much higher in the other three: 18.2% in Italy, 21.6% in France and 23.9% in Spain.

Where is the unemployment gap between age groups widest?

But comparing youth unemployment rates across countries does not show the full picture. Youth unemployment may be low by European standards and still be high compared with the rate in the older age group in the same country.

There are two ways to measure this gap. One is the difference between the two rates in percentage points. The other is a ratio, the youth rate divided by the rate in the older age group, which shows how many times as high the youth rate is.

Romania has the widest gap on both measures. The difference is 25.5 percentage points, and the youth rate is 5.9 times the rate in the older age group.

In Croatia and the UK, the youth rate is at least five times the rate in the older age group. Youth unemployment is 20% in Croatia and 15.6% in the UK, compared with 3.8% and 3.1%, respectively, in the older age group.

Low youth unemployment can still mask a wide gap

Some countries with fairly low youth unemployment still have a wide gap. In Poland, the youth rate is 11.8%, but the rate in the older age group is only 2.8%. In Czechia, the rates are 10.4% and 2.6%. In Norway, they are 13% and 3.1%, respectively. In all three, the youth rate is around four times the rate in the older age group.

In other countries, unemployment is relatively high in both age groups, but the relative gap is smaller. For instance, Spain has one of the highest youth unemployment rates, at 23.9%, but the rate among 25- to 74-year-olds is also high, at 9%. That puts the youth rate at 2.7 times the rate in the older age group, below the EU ratio of three. In Greece, the youth rate is 18.4%, compared with 7.7% in the older age group, giving a ratio of 2.4.

Higher youth unemployment is normal, but the gap matters

Experts say part of the gap is normal. “A combination of factors makes it ‘natural’ that the youth unemployment rate is higher than the adult unemployment rate,” Sara Elder, head of the Employment Analysis and Economic Policy Unit at the International Labour Organization (ILO), told Euronews Business.

She noted that lack of experience is a leading reason. Young people often know less about the labour market and have less experience of looking for work. Employers may choose someone with more experience instead.

Young people may also take time to "shop around" for the right job. Measurement plays a role too. Young people who stay in education longer and are neither working nor looking for work are outside the labour force. So are those who give up looking for a job. Both groups are left out when the youth unemployment rate is calculated.

When fewer young people are in work, the same number of jobseekers makes up a larger share of the youth labour force. That can help explain part of the gap between the two age groups.

Young people also tend to be the last to be hired and the first to lose their jobs in a downturn. "Youth are more vulnerable than adults in difficult economic times," Elder said.

Like young couples, young workers break up more often

"Part of the gap is natural. Young people are at the start of their careers," Professor Michael Siegenthaler, head of the Labour Market Research Division at KOF Swiss Economic Institute at ETH Zurich, told Euronews Business.

He underlined that young people move from education into work, try out different jobs and look for the right match. This search takes time.

Juan J. Dolado, honorary professor at the Carlos III University of Madrid, compared it to personal life. "Just as romantic relationships break up more frequently when people are young, the same is true for employment relationships between firms and workers," he said.

He emphasised that young people often do not fully understand their first jobs, and employers need time to see what these workers can do.

What is a normal gap?

Elder says the ratio can help identify where young jobseekers face extra barriers.

"Given the different systemic tendencies of each cohort, a ratio of the youth-to-adult unemployment rate that falls in the range of 2 to 3 could be considered a natural base. Ratios above 3, however, suggest the presence of a particular hardship (or hardships) faced by young people in their job search compared to adults," Elder said.

She noted that the extremely low ratios in Austria, Germany and Switzerland reflect how well these countries support young people as they move from school or training into work.

“This happens most visibly in their dual track education systems and subsidised apprenticeship programmes for young people following technical fields,” she said.

Siegenthaler added that unlike more school-based education systems, apprenticeships combine classroom learning with training inside a company in these countries. 

Dolado pointed out that the ratio tends to be much higher in countries where the main way for youngsters to access the labour market is via short-term temporary contracts, which lead to high staff turnover.

He warned that this can have a long-term impact. Dismissals or very short contracts can leave "scarring effects" on young people's future careers, he said.
